title: The tree on the riverbank
hookLine: life is a tree on the riverbank; how long can it stand (Farid salok)

lines: THE RIVER WORKS AT THE BANK.
A STRONG TREE ON THE EDGE.
cards: Rivers in the Punjab move. In the rains they swell, and the water works at the banks all season, carrying the soil away a little at a time.

A tree right on the edge can look strong for years: thick trunk, wide shade, birds in it. But its roots are in earth the river is slowly taking. Farid looked at a tree like that and saw something about every life.

teach.h: HOW LONG CAN THE TREE HOLD FIRM?
teach.b: The couplet, on Ang 1382, in paraphrase: a little tree on the riverbank, how long can it hold firm? Farid, in an unbaked clay pot, how long can water be kept? Two pictures, one question, and he doesn't answer it.
Farid's word is rukhra, which some readers hear as the little tree, a tender word. He isn't sneering, and the couplet says nothing against the tree.
The trouble is where every tree stands, on ground that's being carried off. The second picture comes from a potter's yard. A pot that hasn't been fired in the kiln looks like a pot.
You can pour water into it. But the water softens the clay from the inside, and before long it seeps out, or the pot gives way. Farid sets the body there: soft clay, holding something for a while.

teach.h: NOT GLOOM: WHAT WILL YOU DO WITH THE TIME?
teach.b: Read beside his other saloks, it sounds more like a friend's warning, with a practical question: since the bank won't hold forever, what will you do with the time?
Earlier in these days he called himself to rise and pray before dawn; now we can hear why he didn't put it off.
Sikhs hear the same note in the Gurus' teaching that a human life is a precious chance, not to be slept through. The tree on the edge isn't a reason for fear.
It's a reason to stand well, today, while it stands.

how: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of Gurbani; Sikhs hear in them the Gurus' own reminder that human life is short and precious, a chance to remember the Name.

o: a clay pot fired hard in a potter's kiln to hold water
the Punjab's monsoon rains that swell the rivers each year
a little tree on a riverbank, its ground slowly washing away

games.q: inside the couplet — tap the pairs.
p: how long can it hold firm?
how long can it keep water?

s: Farid says the tree is weak
the couplet says nothing against the tree; the trouble is the ground it stands on.
the couplet pairs the tree with an unbaked clay pot
two pictures, one question: how long?

games.q: you're a tree on the riverbank, strong and giving shade, and the river is slowly taking the bank. what does Farid's question point you toward?
o: pretend the bank will hold forever.
stand well and use the time while you stand.
games.why: Farid asks how long the tree can hold firm, and read with his other saloks, it's a friend's warning: don't put off what matters.

practice: If you can, stand near water, a sink, a glass, a window with rain; if not, picture the riverbank.

Stand with your feet planted like the tree, feel your weight on the ground, and let the question come without any fear in it: while I'm standing, what's worth doing today? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Rukhra. Farid's little tree on the riverbank: strong, giving shade, and standing on ground the river is slowly taking.

carryVoice: Your line: how long can it stand. Long enough to stand well. See you tomorrow.
